extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patentees, patent agents, and lawyers practising under UK patent law (Patents Acts 1883–1888)
extracted.subtask_description: Index/excerpt from a patentees' manual summarising substantive legal standards and procedural requirements under UK patent law (Patents Acts 1883–1888), for applicants, agents and litigators. Covers construction, patentability, procedure, remedies, fees, office practice and international arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification to be construed according to ordinary meaning; with reference to state of knowledge when it was prepared; benevolent construction; both words and drawings looked at; prior specifications as showing anticipation; evidence to explain technical terms; patentee's evidence as to meaning of specification inadmissible; claims, construction of, with reference to whole context; when two meanings possible; construed as merely appendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation relies on ordinary meaning and the contemporaneous state of knowledge; read specification as a whole (words + drawings); courts may adopt a benevolent construction; prior specifications can show anticipation; technical terms may be explained by evidence but the patentee's own testimony on meaning is inadmissible; claims are construed in context and, where ambiguous, may be treated as appendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for letters patent to be valid
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent must show that the invention possesses utility, display novelty, show some measure of ingenuity, that the patentee is the true and first inventor (unless communicated from abroad), and that the specification be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid patent requires utility (usefulness), novelty (newness), inventive contribution above triviality, correct ownership/entitlement, and a sufficient specification (complete specification describing and claiming the invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject-matter / invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every kind of thing patentable; what is patentable set out (classes of patentable inventions); amount of invention required to support patent — very small may be sufficient; cases where invention insufficient; must be useful; one invention per patent; importer of an invention may be grantee; alternative devices to effect same object are one invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject-matter limits and utility are substantive bars. Small improvements can suffice if inventive; a patent is to be for one invention (though objections on this ground are limited procedurally). Importers and first producers in commerce may be treated as inventors in some circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is a necessary element of patentable invention; if any part claimed as invention not novel, patent void; novelty is defeated by prior public user, publication, prior specifications, or prior secret user for profit; onus of proving want of novelty lies on defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defeating novelty can be via prior publication, prior public use, earlier specifications, or prior commercial secret use by another. Courts place onus on alleged infringer to prove lack of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention must be useful; question of utility is for the court (or appropriate tribunal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of utility can invalidate a patent; in proceedings (e.g., for extension) non-use may create a presumption against utility but this can be rebutted by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of specification / disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete specification must describe the invention sufficiently; question whether specification describes material with sufficient accuracy is for the court; complete specification should disclose improvements (in complicated machines point them out distinctly); if complete specification describes or claims invention other than that in provisional it is a ground of opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications must enable the skilled reader to practise the invention; divergence between provisional and complete specifications can be a basis for opposition; courts decide sufficiency and identity with prior specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction of claims with reference to whole context; where two meanings possible, principles for construction; claims may be construed as merely appendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are read in light of specification and drawings; ambiguities resolved by reference to specification and the state of knowledge; some claims may be interpreted narrowly as appendant or limited to embodiments described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings to accompany specification, if required; complete specification may refer to those in provisional; drawings not to be referred to as descriptive of part not described in letterpress of specification; omitted drawings by inadvertence cannot be supplied; erroneous drawings will not in all cases vitiate patent; amendment of drawings allowed in certain cases; rules as to drawings provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide drawings whenever required; do not use drawings to claim matter not described in text; correct/erroneous or omitted drawings have prescribed remedies but may be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to grant of patent — grounds and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppositions must be given within prescribed time (notice within two months of advertisement of acceptance) and state grounds; evidence in opposition by statutory declarations; onus of proof lies on opponent; comptroller may hear parties and may allow amendment in notice of opposition; grounds of opposition are limited (1) applicant obtained invention from opponent or legal representative, (2) invention already patented in this country on a prior application date, (3) complete specification describes or claims an invention other than that in the provisional and such other invention is subject of opponent's application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition practice is formal: timely notice, stated grounds, statutory-declaration evidence, possible amendment, hearing before Comptroller, limited grounds, and rules regulate proceedings; in cases of doubt patent may be granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller-General powers and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Comptroller may require amendment of documents, require statements in writing from applicant, authorise amendment of specification, refuse patent if contrary to law or morality, correct clerical errors, may require parties to be heard before exercising adverse discretion, must notify decisions to parties, has general powers of amendment, may dispense with evidence, may apply to law officers for directions, certificate of comptroller to be evidence, issues illustrated journal and reports, make annual report, may appoint officer if absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comptroller has broad administrative powers over prosecution, amendment and publication; must follow procedural fairness (opportunity to be heard) when exercising discretion adversely to applicants; decisions are notified and certain acts produce official evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and payment consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: List of fees prescribed; non-payment within prescribed time renders patent void; comptroller may enlarge time in certain cases; fees may in certain cases be paid on day following due date; rules exist for payment of fees for continuance of patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely payment is critical to maintain patent validity; there are limited remedies (enlargement of time) but failure to pay is a statutory ground for lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of patent and extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration limited to fourteen years from date; may be extended by petition to the Queen in Council (extension may be for up to fourteen years but more than seven requires exceptional merit and public usefulness); procedure and conditions for extension include petitions, notices, caveats, production of accounts, and hearing; extension treated as grant of new patent and is subject to statutory provisions; grant of extension does not decide validity of original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions are discretionary, quasi-judicial proceedings before the Judicial Committee/Privy Council; petitioner must set forth material facts, provide full accounts of profits, show merit and public usefulness, and follow time limits for filing; extensions can carry conditions and are only granted where justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of letters patent — evidence and accounts required
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner should produce all material facts; accounts must be full, clear, unreserved and properly proved; what profits must be shown and what deductions may be made are specified; deductions claimed should appear in petition or accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial proof is central to extension petitions: full account of profits derived from the patent, with proper proof and disclosure of claimed deductions; failure to present adequate accounts may defeat extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence in patent proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence in opposition to grant of patents; to amendments of specifications; on applications for compulsory licences; on applications for extensions; on actions for infringement; official documentary evidence — certified and sealed copies receivable in evidence and to be furnished on payment of fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different types of proceedings have specified evidence procedures (e.g., statutory declarations for opposition). Official certified copies from the Patent Office are admissible evidence across proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — substantive tests and modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes of infringement include substituting chemical or mechanical equivalents, colourable alterations, immaterial alterations to evade a patent, using substantial similarity, where principle is new, whether different process to arrive at same result infringes when the process was described, and treatment of combinations, chemical processes/products and parts; use by others, by agents, and by Crown have specific rules; intention of infringer is not material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement analysis focuses on substance over form: equivalents, substantial part/use, and whether the accused product or process falls within the invention's essential nature; intention is irrelevant; many special rules apply for combinations, processes and chemical matters; liability may extend to dealers and users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies — injunctions and accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff entitled to injunction; interlocutory and perpetual injunctions available where appropriate; injunctions may be granted before trial in proper cases; in some cases plaintiff must give undertaking as to damages; if injunction not granted defendant usually ordered to keep an account; licensee may not apply in name of owner for injunction and cannot ordinarily sue alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable relief (injunctions) is a primary remedy for infringement; courts balance equities (undertakings, interim relief) and may order accounts or damages instead depending on case circumstances and innocence of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs in patent proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Comptroller and Board of Trade have limited authority to award costs; law officer may order costs in any proceeding before him; costs may be ordered on oppositions, amendments of specifications, applications for extension, revocation actions, actions for threats and infringement; special rules apply where the validity of the patent was in question in prior proceedings affecting later costs awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs awards vary by forum: law officers and courts broadly control costs; administrative officers have limited power; costs consequences can affect subsequent proceedings depending on prior findings/certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition grounds — three main grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds of opposition to grant: (1) applicant obtained invention from opponent or from person of whom he is legal representative; (2) invention patented in this country on application of prior date; (3) complete specification describes or claims invention other than that in provisional and such other invention is subject of opponent's application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents must have standing/interest; oppositions may be founded even on expired prior patents; disclaiming clauses may be required; procedural rules (timing, statutory declarations) are strict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars of breaches and objections in infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Particulars of breaches and of objections must be delivered in actions for infringement (and may be required in actions for threats); particulars may be amended; insufficient particulars may be ordered to be made more specific; evidence outside particulars not admitted except by leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimants must plead and particularise alleged infringing acts and objections; failure to particularise can limit admissible evidence at trial and can attract costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint patentees / joint inventors rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Where joint patentees, each may use the invention; joint patentees may be inventor and non-inventor; one co-owner cannot assign more than his share; joint proprietors' rights and liabilities in assignment/licensing described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint ownership gives each co-owner certain independent rights to exploit; allocations, accounts and assignments are subject to share proportions and may create obligations between co-owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licences and licensee rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Licences should be registered; various forms of licence (including exclusive) exist; registration for a district is not necessarily notice to the world; licensee during licence may not dispute validity of patent (but may seek to have the patentee's rights defined); exclusive licensee for district cannot restrain persons without notice of articles bought outside district; licensees may have payment and covenant obligations; Board of Trade may order compulsory licences in some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful drafting and registration of licences is important; licensee status affects standing to sue, capacity to dispute validity, and territorial effect. Compulsory licence procedure is statutory and distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licences procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Board of Trade may order patentee to grant licences (compulsory licences); procedure involves petition and rules regulating proceedings; forms of application and opposition provided; orders of Board of Trade for compulsory licences are absolute and final for patents under certain Acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsory licences are administrative remedies available under statute with prescribed forms and opposition rights; outcomes are final subject to statutory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Convention / foreign patents / right of priority
rubrics_metrics.description: International Convention arrangements govern foreign applications and rights of priority of foreign applicants; publication in England of complete specification may bar foreign rights; patents under the Convention only granted in England to person making foreign application; Act applies even if foreign state acceded after date of foreign application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International priority and exhibition rules affect filing strategy; foreign applications and priority must be coordinated with domestic publication to preserve rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments, public use and exhibition protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments abandoned do not avoid subsequent patent; experiments by inventor are not publication provided they make no profitable use; authorised use at exhibitions is protected under the International Convention if proper notice filed; experiments made to procure evidence for trial are distrusted by courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private experimental use by the inventor may not destroy novelty, but commercial/authorised use or publication can; special protection exists for exhibition displays under international rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official documents and certified copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Certified and sealed copies of Patent Office documents are receivable in evidence and to be furnished on payment of fee; sent to Scotland, Ireland and the Isle of Man and to be evidence in courts there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use certified Patent Office copies as primary documentary evidence in litigation and official proceedings; fees apply for copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost patent / duplicate patent procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: If original patent lost or destroyed, duplicate may be granted; form of application for duplicate set out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a statutory procedure to replace lost/destroyed patents (application, forms, possible publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent agents and privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications between inventor and his patent agent are not privileged; persons describing themselves as patent agents when not on the register liable to penalty; Institute/registration of patent agents, rules and registers maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use registered patent agents; communications with agents do not have legal privilege and unregistered representation can attract penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents Office registers, publications and library
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Office maintains registers, publications, indexes, an Illustrated Journal and a public library and Patent Museum; registers and indexes of specifications and patents are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office publications and indexes are key resources for searching novelty, publication records, and for procedural notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for mislabelling and misuse of royal arms
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties exist for describing goods as patented when no patent has been granted for the same, for using word 'patent' incorrectly on labels, for use of royal arms without authority, and penalties under the Merchandise Marks Act 1887.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure accurate marking and avoid false claims of patent protection; statutory penalties and civil remedies may apply for misrepresentation.
